items.stem: An underwriting step carries no licensing requirement, but success is measured by loss ratio, not final until claims mature twelve months later. The program owner needs a performance view before quarterly review. What should the team do?

opts.t: Delay automating the step until twelve months of loss-ratio data confirm it performs as intended.
Automate the step now and track a fast proxy — override or reopen rate — until loss ratio matures.
Automate the step, but report performance only for the subset of claims that have already closed.
Route the step to a licensed underwriter for sign-off, with the model preparing a draft recommendation.

items.whyRight: The step's own fit signals already support automation; only the outcome metric is slow to arrive, and the stem states no licensing requirement blocks it. A fast proxy — override or reopen rate — gives a defensible interim reading before loss ratio matures.

whyWrong.A: Feedback latency calls for a proxy signal, not a delay; the step's fit signals already support automating it now, before the loss ratio matures.
whyWrong.C: Restricting reporting to already-closed claims abandons the majority still open; the proxy signal, not a narrower scope, is what supplies the missing interim measurement.
whyWrong.D: The step carries no licensing requirement, so routing it to a licensed underwriter for sign-off answers a condition the stem explicitly rules out.

items.factAnswerRaw: Automate, with a proxy signal (override rate, reopen rate)

items.stem: A document-processing pipeline must complete a compliance redaction step before a document enters the search index; auditors require this order hold on every run, not just typically. Which mechanism should enforce it?

opts.t: A programmatic precondition that blocks indexing until the redaction step returns a completion signal.
A JSON output contract carrying an explicit confidence field for the downstream service to route on.
Strengthened system-prompt instructions directing the model to always redact documents before indexing them.
Few-shot examples demonstrating the correct redact-then-index sequence for the model to imitate.

items.whyRight: Step ordering here is a correctness requirement, not a typical case; only a programmatic precondition enforces it deterministically every run. Prompt instructions, few-shot examples, and output-routing contracts all leave room for the sequence to be skipped.

whyWrong.B: A confidence field helps a downstream service route on the model's output; it does nothing to guarantee redaction actually runs before indexing occurs.
whyWrong.C: Prompt instructions are probabilistic; a rule stated clearly enough still fails on the runs where the ordering matters most, which is what auditors require against.
whyWrong.D: Examples raise the odds the model imitates the correct order; they do not guarantee it, and a guarantee is what an audited sequencing requirement needs.

items.t1Clause: must complete a compliance redaction step before a document enters the search index; auditors require this order hold on every run
items.factAnswerRaw: Programmatic precondition blocking B until A returns

items.stem: A support system classifies each incoming ticket into one of five known categories, then dispatches to a category-specific handler. Roughly 40,000 tickets arrive daily, and the team is evaluating an agent framework. Which pattern fits the requirement?

opts.t: A single agent that decides at runtime which handler each ticket needs.
A workflow that routes each classified ticket to its matching handler.
A coordinator dispatching to five specialist subagents, one per category.
A single large prompt handling every category's logic in one call.

items.whyRight: The five categories are known and enumerable, so the routing decision belongs in code; a workflow dispatches each classified ticket to its handler at a fraction of the cost and latency variance any agentic or multi-agent alternative would add across all 40,000 daily tickets.

whyWrong.A: Runtime discovery is the cost that funds an agent, and nothing here is undiscovered; the five categories are already enumerated, so an agent adds variance for no stated benefit.
whyWrong.C: Splitting five known branches across a coordinator and five subagents multiplies token spend roughly 4-5x for a routing decision that a single workflow already handles cleanly.
whyWrong.D: One monolithic call mixing five categories' logic dilutes attention across all of them at once, where the workflow's separate handlers keep each category's logic isolated.

items.stem: In a hub-and-spoke multi-agent system, the coordinator owns decomposition and must partition the space before delegating. On a fixed token budget, two subagents investigated the same source cluster, each returning correct results. Which two actions fix the root cause? Select two.

opts.t: Have the coordinator partition the research space into non-overlapping segments before dispatching any subagent.
Give the coordinator an explicit map assigning each subagent a distinct segment of the space.
Add a deduplication pass after the subagents return, to merge overlapping findings.
Add structured error propagation so one subagent's failure no longer terminates the whole run.

items.whyRight: Two subagents covering the same ground traces to the coordinator's decomposition, not to either subagent's execution — both returned correct results. Partitioning the space before delegating and mapping each subagent to a distinct segment both fix that upstream cause directly.

whyWrong.C: Deduplicating after the subagents return treats the symptom once tokens are already spent; it does not stop the coordinator from assigning overlapping ground on the next run.
whyWrong.D: Structured error propagation prevents one subagent's crash from ending the run; nothing here failed — both subagents returned correct results, they simply covered the same ground.

items.t1Clause: two subagents investigated the same source cluster
items.factAnswerRaw: Coordinator did not partition the space before delegating

items.stem: A code-security review runs per-file local scans, then a synthesis pass surfaces cross-file vulnerabilities; only structured summaries should cross that seam. Under a fixed audit deadline, the synthesis pass now receives the raw diff of all 40 files. What should change?

opts.t: Give the synthesis pass a larger context window so it can process all 40 raw diffs at once.
Instruct the synthesis pass's prompt to carefully cross-reference all 40 raw diffs for consistency.
Merge the local-scan and synthesis passes into one combined pass over all 40 files.
Replace the raw diffs with each file's structured local-scan summary as the integration pass's input.

items.whyRight: The seam between local scans and synthesis is defined to carry structured summaries; raw diffs reintroduce exactly the attention dilution the two-pass split existed to remove. Swapping in each file's structured summary restores the seam without adding a bigger model, a second pass, or more prose.

whyWrong.A: A larger context window still processes 40 raw diffs at once; capacity was never the constraint, and dilution persists at any window size until the input itself changes.
whyWrong.B: Prompt instructions asking the synthesis pass to cross-reference more carefully still hand it 40 raw diffs to dilute its attention across; the input format is the defect, not the instructions.
whyWrong.C: Merging the two passes recreates the single monolithic review the two-pass split was designed to prevent; the defect here is the seam's data format, not too many stages.

items.t1Clause: runs per-file local scans, then a synthesis pass
items.factAnswerRaw: Pass the structured per-file summaries instead

items.stem: Total cost — inference plus human review time — is the named pillar for a pipeline classifying 200,000 items monthly. A redesign halves per-call inference cost using a smaller model, but doubles the volume routed to human reviewers. What should the team do?

opts.t: Approve the redesign; a smaller model is a clear efficiency win regardless of downstream review load.
Approve the redesign, and add a monitoring dashboard tracking the growing human review backlog.
Approve the redesign, and hire additional reviewers to absorb the doubled review volume.
Reject the redesign; total cost rises because the extra human review time outweighs the inference savings.

items.whyRight: Total cost is the named pillar, and it includes both inference and human review time, not inference alone. Halving inference spend while doubling reviewer volume moves the metric the wrong way overall, so the redesign is a net regression that should be rejected outright.

whyWrong.A: Efficiency on the inference side is only half of the named pillar; the doubled human review time is the other half, and it grows faster than the model savings shrink.
whyWrong.B: A dashboard shows the review backlog growing; it does not lower total cost, which is still rising because the underlying trade was never reversed.
whyWrong.C: Hiring reviewers to absorb the doubled volume adds its own cost on top of the trade already made, moving total cost further in the wrong direction, not back down.

items.t1Clause: doubles the volume routed to human reviewers

notes: g5: shape substituted S5 -> S1. F-1.11-02 ('pass structured summaries, not raw payloads, across a seam') is a named-principle-violation fact, not a ladder-rung (workflow/agent) selection, so S1 fits the facet's actual content better than the assigned S5.

All six items' T1 pivots resolve to a real, nameable row in their own section's decision/symptom table (verified against CCAR-P_Domain-1_v1.md before shipping): g1->1.1 row 3 (licensed decision), g2->1.10 row 4 (JSON routing contract), g3->1.3 row 3 (non-enumerable/agent), g4->1.6 row 4 (structured error propagation), g5->1.11 row 5 (merge over-split steps), g6-> the converse of F-1.12-03's own stated 'regression' reasoning. None flagged as IRREDUCIBLE this batch.

Distractor scenarios for g1, g2, g3, and g5 were deliberately built around new concrete situations (insurance program review, document-redaction ordering, ticket routing, code-security review) rather than the corpus's own 'Exam scenario' illustrations for those sections, per the brief's different-failure-mode requirement.
